name: CRG Festus
heading: 3. CRG Festus — 600 MW Proposed After Major Redesign
brief: St. Louis-based CRG , a Clayco subsidiary, has scaled down its planned data center outside Festus, Jefferson County , from an initial 1,000 MW concept to roughly 600 MW . The company’s current official project page specifies four single-story data center buildings on about 173 acres of development area, while preserving an estimated 188 acres of woodland . A potential $6 billion investment represents the developer’s expectation over the completed project, not money already spent on an operating facility. The developer’s community information site makes the design change explicit: the original idea called for 12 two-story buildings and approximately 1 GW. CRG says the revised campus would have deeper buffers, a 500-foot setback from residential property lines, closed-loop cooling and an Ameren switchyard. The 600 MW is the current proposed facility scale ; the company has not publicly established that a 600 MW utility service contract is fully energized, nor that 600 MW of critical IT equipment is installed. name: Google Project Mica, Kansas City
heading: 2. Google Project Mica, Kansas City — Nearly 700 MW Under Development
brief: Google confirmed on February 12, 2026 that it was developing Project Mica in Kansas City’s Northland, at the northeast corner of Interstate 435 and U.S. Highway 169 . Port KC’s official development record describes a nearly 500-acre , five-building campus with approximately 1.56 million square feet of data center space. The port authority reports that the full development would draw nearly 700 MW using the adjacent Nashua Power Station and planned on-site substations. That is the most specific publicly attributable site power figure for Project Mica; it is not a record of current IT consumption. Construction was already underway when Google confirmed its role. The port authority had authorized up to $10 billion in taxable revenue bonds , which is a financing ceiling, not evidence that Google has already borrowed or spent that sum. The project also carries a 25-year property-tax exemption arrangement and upfront workforce payments totaling $1.75 million to the Smithville School District and Northland Career Center, according to Port KC. name: Nebius Independence AI Factory
heading: 1. Nebius Independence AI Factory — Up to 1,200 MW Across Planned Power Sources
brief: Nebius is building a roughly 400-acre AI factory near Route 78 and Little Blue Parkway in Independence , east of Kansas City. Its March 3, 2026 announcement followed City Council approval of a Chapter 100 industrial development incentive plan and specified an eventual 1.2 GW campus . On May 12 , the company held a groundbreaking, independently confirmed by the Missouri Department of Economic Development . The first phase is under construction, but the whole 1.2 GW project is not online. The developer’s updated Independence project FAQ provides the power split missing from many summaries: 800 MW from Independence Power & Light and 400 MW of planned on-site generation for later phases. Its utility arrangement involves power provided by a new privately financed facility at the retired Blue Valley Power Plant and energy transactions through the Southwest Power Pool. Nebius says it will pay for infrastructure upgrades and expects residents’ rates to be protected. name: Hyperscale Data, BNI Montana
heading: 3. Hyperscale Data, BNI Montana — 125 MW Additional Power Under Conditional Utility Letter
brief: Hyperscale Data says it has a path to potentially add 125 MW at one of two leased Montana mining sites. In its June 24, 2026 company announcement , subsidiary BNI Montana reported receiving a formal conditional “will serve” letter from Lower Yellowstone Rural Electric Cooperative after a load study. The affected facility operates at approximately 10 MW supporting Bitcoin mining, the company said. Its second Montana site, about 15 miles away, can also operate at roughly 10 MW but has not undergone the same power study. This is 125 MW of possible new supply in addition to the current roughly 10 MW , not 125 MW already energized. If every required investment and approval were secured, the single studied site could theoretically approach about 135 MW of total electrical availability . That is a conditional development scenario, not a signed 135 MW service agreement. Critically, Hyperscale’s June announcement did not publicly identify which of its two Montana leases received the study , so we do not assign the 125 MW letter to a precise parcel or add the same opportunity to both sites. name: Atlas Power, Butte
heading: 2. Atlas Power, Butte — 150 MW Expansion Proposal; 75 MW Existing Operating Site
brief: Atlas Power Group runs one of Montana’s better-established large data centers outside Butte, Silver Bow County . The Montana Department of Environmental Quality’s 2026 data-center information sheet lists the Butte facility at 75 MW of existing operating electricity load. The site primarily supports cryptocurrency mining rather than an announced large AI training installation. For its next stage, utility NorthWestern Energy announced on December 19, 2024 a plan to provide 75 MW of new supply beginning in 2026 , with growth of up to another 75 MW in the following three to five years. The corresponding up-to-150 MW figure is an announced new-service expansion envelope , based on a nonbinding letter of intent . It should not be described as 150 MW of added supply that has already been delivered, or automatically added to the original 75 MW to state a completed 225 MW campus. name: Quantica Big Sky Campus, Broadview
heading: 1. Quantica Big Sky Campus, Broadview — 1,100 MW Proposed; Site Work Advancing
brief: Quantica Infrastructure , through its Big Sky Digital Infrastructure subsidiary, is planning a 1,100 MW data center and integrated power campus across approximately 5,100 acres near Broadview in Yellowstone County . The developer confirmed that scale in its August 31 announcement . The site is roughly 30 miles north of Billings. At full buildout, the company envisions multiple computing buildings, local energy generation and transmission infrastructure. No completed 1,100 MW computing campus or publicly identified anchor cloud tenant was documented in the materials reviewed as of October 29. The project moved forward in a limited but concrete way this week. On October 27 , the Yellowstone County Board of County Commissioners approved a road-use and maintenance agreement by a 3–0 vote . It requires the developer to use designated sections of Heiken and Buffalo Trail roads, improve one mile of gravel access, conduct inspections and post a $250,000 surety bond . name: Monolith and Crusoe, Hallam
heading: 3. Monolith and Crusoe, Hallam — 35 MW Approved
brief: Monolith and Crusoe won approval on October 5, 2026 for a 35-megawatt modular data center on approximately ten acres at Monolith’s existing Olive Creek industrial campus in Hallam, Lancaster County . The Hallam Village Board approved the special-use permit unanimously after months of public meetings, according to Nebraska Public Media . The approval authorizes a planned facility, not an operating 35 MW IT load. The project could give an established industrial site a second economic purpose. Crusoe has experience operating modular computing infrastructure and building larger AI campuses elsewhere. The companies have discussed roughly 15 permanent jobs and local benefit payments. KLKN’s account of the approved arrangement says Crusoe would provide $1 million when the project begins operating , followed by $150,000 annually for ten years . Those payments are contingent on the development reaching its milestones. name: MARA Minden
heading: 2. MARA Minden — 42 MW Existing Grid-Connected Site
brief: MARA Holdings acquired a 42 MW nameplate-capacity data center in central Nebraska in January 2026 , expanding its operating mining infrastructure. MARA’s current portfolio identifies the facility as Minden, Nebraska , on approximately seven acres . Its first-quarter SEC filing distinguishes 35 MW of operating Bitcoin-mining capacity from the site’s 42 MW nameplate . The higher number is the installed facility’s rated capacity, not evidence of continuous 42 MW consumption. MARA has argued that energized sites and low-cost power provide a starting point for future high-performance computing. Its January acquisition adds equipment, electrical infrastructure and operating experience without requiring an entirely new greenfield site. That can reduce development risk and create an opportunity for additional computing investment if suitable customers, cooling and network upgrades follow. It does not mean the Minden mining facility has already been converted into a large AI training center. name: MARA and Starwood Project Horizon, Kearney
heading: 1. MARA and Starwood Project Horizon, Kearney — Up to 368 MW Planned
brief: MARA and Starwood Digital Ventures are working on Project Horizon , a multistage data center redevelopment at Kearney’s Tech oNE Crossing business park. The official project website describes a 100 MW first phase using electricity already available to the adjacent Bitcoin mining operation. MARA’s corporate site gives 368 MW as the location’s longer-term gross potential, subject to expansion. The 368 MW is a development pathway, not a completed AI data center or 368 MW of newly contracted electricity. The Kearney City Council approved the project’s conditional-use permit in September, after the city adopted tighter rules on data centers. The plan would construct enclosed data halls in stages and ultimately retire the older outdoor Bitcoin-mining operation. Local coverage of the city’s September hearing identifies the full 368 MW figure, while the developer describes approximately 72 acres for its initial business-park development. name: Copia Power Monarch, Mason Valley
heading: 3. Copia Power Monarch, Mason Valley — 1,000 MW Proposed
brief: Copia Power is proposing a 1,000 MW data center development across approximately 505 acres north of Yerington in Lyon County’s Mason Valley. On August 6, 2026 , the Lyon County Board of County Commissioners approved a planned-unit-development zoning change by a 3–1 vote, with one abstention . The proposal encompasses up to 4.6 million square feet across eight two-story data center buildings, electrical infrastructure and supporting facilities. This is a significant advance for a project seeking to diversify an agricultural region’s economy. Large computing customers could create construction jobs, utility investment and a new commercial tax base. In October reporting from The Nevada Independent , landowner Brian Masini described the prospect of development as an economic opportunity for a community struggling to sustain traditional farming. A new high-value industrial use can be attractive when agricultural margins and local services are under pressure. The county’s vote did not authorize construction . name: Tract South Valley Technology Park
heading: 2. Tract South Valley Technology Park — 1,215 MW Ultimate Potential
brief: Tract markets its South Valley Technology Park in Storey County at 1,215 MW of eventual campus capacity across approximately 1,534 acres . Unlike many speculative land banks, a substantial first project is genuinely underway. Its affiliated builder Fleet Data Centers broke ground in May 2026 on a leased facility within the park near USA Parkway at the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center. The first South Valley data center is described in public financing and development reporting as a roughly 230 MW turnkey facility , including about 200 MW of critical computing power . This is a separate, far smaller figure than the 1,215 MW full-park potential. Fleet’s separate Peru Ridge project is another campus and is not added to South Valley’s capacity. Data Center Dynamics reported the groundbreaking, a long-term lease to an unnamed investment-grade tenant and the first project’s financing. name: Tract Virginia Highlands
heading: 1. Tract Virginia Highlands — 2,500 MW Marketed Development Capacity
brief: Tract lists its Virginia Highlands Technology Park in Storey County at a potential 2,500 MW of future data center capacity, making it the largest single marketed development park with an explicit owner-published MW figure in this comparison. The 8,590-acre property sits between the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center and Virginia City Highlands and is divided into 11 parcels ranging from about 250 to 1,200 acres. Its industrial zoning supports future computing and energy infrastructure. Tract’s June 18, 2024 acquisition announcement established that the land purchase had closed earlier that year. The company’s current project page identifies the site as owned and in development . Those are meaningful commitments: Tract has secured control of the property and is marketing it for data center uses. They are not proof that 2.5 gigawatts of grid service has been contracted, buildings financed, tenants signed or computing racks energized. name: FirstLight Manchester
heading: 3. FirstLight Manchester — 2 MW Fully Built-Out Capacity, Operating
brief: At 77 Sundial Avenue in Manchester , FirstLight Fiber operates one of New Hampshire’s documented commercial colocation facilities. Independent industry directory Data Center Map lists 2 MW of fully built-out power and approximately 15,000 square feet of available white-space capacity. FirstLight’s own facility page specifies 14,400 square feet , a Tier 2-standard configuration, two utility power feeds, dual uninterruptible power supplies and a backup generator. The area figures are not necessarily measured on identical bases. The data center serves the practical needs of companies that require secure rack space, power backup and fiber connectivity rather than a single vast AI training installation. FirstLight describes a regional fiber network connecting its colocation locations across the Northeast. This existing operation is more mature than either New Hampshire proposal in the ranking, even though its published megawatt capacity is much lower. A fully built-out power specification is a facility-design or service-capacity figure, not proof that every megawatt is continuously used.

name: Concord Locke Road
heading: 2. Concord Locke Road — Roughly 15 MW Proposed, Decision Deferred
brief: The City of Concord’s public application identifies a proposed 8,160-square-foot building at 52 Locke Road , including approximately 7,220 square feet of data center space , an office, garage and caretaker residence. Northpoint Engineering submitted the plan for landowner Granite Municipal Manufacturing & Sales. AI infrastructure company Levitate is providing the design and cooling approach. Levitate CEO Ryan Howard describes the design as part of a 15 MW class of micro data centers using single-phase immersion cooling. In October 26 reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio and the Concord Monitor , Howard estimated approximately 13.5 MW of IT power , excluding overhead electrical use. Those figures are related but not interchangeable: 13.5 MW describes the prospective servers, while approximately 15 MW describes the wider facility class. Neither is measured operating demand. The application is real, but it has not won final approval. brief: The largest number attached to a possible New Hampshire data center concerns the retired Merrimack Station site in Bow . Owner Granite Shore Power requested a preliminary grid feasibility assessment involving Eversource and a potential 350 MW electrical connection . New Hampshire Bulletin’s September reporting and WMUR’s review of the filings established that the regulatory paperwork does not explicitly identify a data center or even definitively designate the proposed facility’s location. The reason Bow appears in this ranking is the connection between those filings and publicly acknowledged local discussions about a possible large data center. New Hampshire Consumer Advocate Donald Kreis also relayed a utility executive’s mention of a project of up to 200 MW . This is a separate account of a possible data-center size, not confirmation that the project’s final capacity will be 200 MW or 350 MW. name: QTS East Windsor
heading: 3. QTS East Windsor — 70 MW-Plus Campus, Operating and Expanding
brief: QTS Data Centers lists 70 MW-plus of critical power capacity at its East Windsor campus, located at 159 Princeton-Hightstown Road in Mercer County. The site already serves business-continuity and disaster-recovery customers in the Northeast corridor and has its own substation. QTS is proposing an additional data center building, but has not published a separately confirmed megawatt addition for that building. The company’s community information page puts the proposed expansion investment at approximately $600 million , with expectations of around 400 construction jobs and five to eight permanent jobs . QTS also operates an approximately 14 MW solar installation associated with the campus. That figure describes generating capacity, not additional server load, and is not added to the 70 MW-plus rating. name: Meta Los Lunas
heading: 3. Meta Los Lunas — 118 MW Estimated Operating IT Power
brief: Meta’s Los Lunas data center in Valencia County is the most mature large computing operation in this comparison. Opened in 2019, it has grown through successive expansions and now includes AI infrastructure. The campus is real and operational, although Meta has not published a directly comparable public megawatt figure for its current server load. Independent research group Epoch AI estimated on October 26, 2026 that Los Lunas supports about 118 MW of operating IT power , with a projection of 218 MW by the first quarter of 2028 . Epoch derives those estimates from satellite imagery, construction timelines, cooling-equipment assumptions and hardware models. They are useful engineering estimates, not utility-meter readings, company specifications or a verified energization schedule . The future number could change as construction and hardware plans evolve. The expansion’s electricity arrangements have a separate public record.
